title: Arjuna joins his palms
hookLine: before God's universal form, Arjuna joins his palms; at an arrivals gate, a grandmother does the same
carry: anjali: one bow for God, elders and guests
tomorrow: Why does Shiva teach without a word?

lines: PALMS TOGETHER, A DIP OF THE HEAD.
A MUDRA, HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.
cards: The arrivals gate at an airport, late in the evening. A tired young man comes through the sliding doors pulling a suitcase.
An older woman at the rail sees him, and before she hugs him, before she says his name, she presses her palms together in front of her chest and dips her head. He does it back. Then the hug.
Two seconds, maybe less, and nobody around them notices. That small shape of the hands is a mudra, so familiar it's easy to forget it is one.

teach.b: The gesture has a name: anjali. Two palms joined, fingers pointing up, usually held at the chest, sometimes at the forehead.
Anjali can also mean the cupped hollow of two hands, the shape you'd make to carry water or flowers as an offering. So the joined palms carry a sense of offering.

teach.h: NAMASTE: THE WORDS. A BOW TO YOU.
teach.b: And namaste? That's not the gesture. It's the words said with it: namas, a bow; te, to you.

Now watch the Bhagavad Gita use this mudra at its most overwhelming moment. In chapter eleven, Arjuna has been given the divine eye and sees Krishna's universal form, vast, blazing, with many faces and eyes.
The text tells us what his body does.
In paraphrase: filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, Arjuna bowed his head, joined his palms, and spoke.
Later, trembling, palms still joined, he bows again and speaks in a choking voice, bowing to Krishna in front, behind, on every side. Notice what the text shows first. Not Arjuna's thoughts.
His hands. Before God, the hands go first. And here's the teaching that carries that bow off the battlefield.

teach.h: MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST: AS GOD.
teach.b: The Taittiriya Upanishad sends its students home with a list, in paraphrase: let your mother be a god to you, your father a god, your teacher a god, your guest a god.

teach.h: ONE BOW, FOR GOD AND FOR NANI.
teach.b: That's why the same joined palms greet the murti in the shrine and the grandmother at the door. In this teaching, the divine is honored in the people in front of you, and anjali is how the hands say it.

how: In Hindu homes and temples, people greet the deity, elders, teachers and guests with anjali, palms joined at the chest, often with the words namaste or namaskar and a slight bow of the head.

o: a breath held while kneeling before a shrine
the words said aloud while bowing to an elder
seals or gestures, like palms joined in offering

games.q: the joined palms — tap the pairs.
p: palms joined, the shape of offering
bowed his head and joined his palms
mother, father, teacher, guest as god

s: namaste is the name of the gesture
the gesture is anjali; namaste is the words said with it, a bow to you.
in the Gita, Arjuna joins his palms before Krishna's universal form
in chapter eleven, filled with wonder, he bows his head and joins his palms.
anjali is only for the deity, never for people
the Taittiriya Upanishad says let mother, father, teacher and guest be as god, so the same bow greets them.

games.q: you're Arjuna, seeing Krishna's universal form, vast and blazing. what does the text show you doing first?
o: bowing your head and joining your palms.
games.why: the Gita shows his body before his words: hair standing on end, head bowed, palms joined. Then he speaks.

practice: Bring the palms together in front of the chest, fingers pointing up, thumbs resting lightly near the breastbone, and let the head dip a little.

Bring to mind an elder, a teacher or a guest, and hold the gesture toward them for a few breaths, as the Upanishad says: as you would toward God. If you pray, offer the same bow to the deity you love.
If the arms tire, let the hands rest in the lap and keep the feeling.

wordCard.voice: The mudras. Today, anjali: two palms joined in offering, the same bow for God, for elders and for guests.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: anjali, the joined or cupped hands, a gesture of offering and respect.

carryVoice: Your line: anjali: one bow for God, elders and guests. Tomorrow, a teacher who says nothing at all. Go gently.
